title: Little Lord Fauntleroy

subtitle.text: On a hot July morning, a carriage drove through a run-down section of New York City.
Inside the carriage sat a tall, thin Englishman named Mr. Havisham.
"I've been the earl's lawyer for forty years," he said to himself.
"But I've never had an assignment like this."
The elderly man scowled as he surveyed the rows of narrow brick houses on the dirty streets.
"The earl wants me to find his grandson and take the boy back to England."
Mr. Havisham shook his head.
"I can't believe Lord Fauntleroy, the earl's heir, lives here in this shabby neighborhood!"
The Earl of Dorincourt was a wealthy, bad-tempered man who hated America and Americans.
He suffered from gout, a painful disease that only increased his foul moods.
He'd had two sons. His older son, Bevis Errol, had been a constant disappointment.
The earl had briefly approved of his younger son, a captain in the army.
But then Captain Errol went to the United States and married an American woman.
The earl was sure she'd only married him for his money.
Furious, the earl cut off communication and refused to give the couple any money.
That was many years ago. In the meantime both Bevis and Captain Errol had died.
This meant that Cedric Errol, the captain's nine-year-old son, was Lord Fauntleroy.
"I can't imagine how rude and ignorant the boy is." Mr. Havisham shuddered.
"And I dread dealing with his greedy mother."
The carriage passed a grocery store, turned the corner, and stopped in front of a modest house.
A servant led Mr. Havisham into a plain but neat parlor.
While he waited, he looked around the room.
"There's not much here, but everything—the furniture, the pictures—is in good taste," Mr. Havisham thought.
"Of course that's probably the captain's influence and not his wife's.
He wouldn't have wanted things that looked cheap even if they were inexpensive."
A few minutes later, a woman in a black dress entered the room.
"I'm sorry to have kept you waiting," Mrs. Errol said.
"I . . . I mean . . ." For a moment the lawyer could barely speak.
He hadn't expected the widow to be so young or so pretty.
Her simple dress was in perfectly good taste.
Perhaps she was responsible for decorating the parlor after all.
Mr. Havisham looked into her sad eyes.
"The earl was wrong," Mr. Havisham thought.
"I'm a good judge of character. This woman didn't marry Captain Errol for his money.
She loved him and still mourns him after all these years."
When Mr. Havisham explained why he had come, Mrs. Errol turned pale.
"Do you have to take Cedric away?" Mrs. Errol clasped a hand to her mouth.
"We love each other so much! You don't know what he means to me.
He's all I have since his father died.
Cedric was so young when that happened . . . why does he have to go now?"
Mr. Havisham cleared his throat. The tears in Mrs. Errol's eyes made him uncomfortable.
"The earl feels it's time for Lord Fauntleroy to begin training for his future role.
Obviously that's not something he can do here." The lawyer looked around the humble room.
"Cedric will live with the earl in Dorincourt Castle."
Mrs. Errol's voice trembled. "He's too young to be so far away from me."
"Of course you will accompany your son to England."
Mrs. Errol relaxed slightly.
"The earl will provide a house for you near the castle as well as a suitable allowance.
Lord Fauntleroy will be permitted to visit you.
But I must emphasize . . ." Mr. Havisham paused.
"The earl doesn't feel kindly toward you.
He does not want to see you, and you are forbidden to enter the castle grounds."
Mr. Havisham was afraid Mrs. Errol would sob and make a scene.
But she simply went to the window.
For a few minutes, she stood with her back to him. Then she turned.
"My husband was very fond of Dorincourt Castle," she said.
"He loved England and everything English.
He would want Cedric to know his old home.
And he would want Cedric to receive the best possible education for a future earl."
"I'm glad you agree!" Mr. Havisham was pleased with how easily the conversation had gone.
He was also impressed that Mrs. Errol hadn't asked about the size of her allowance.
"Cedric has always been loved in this house. I'm sure the earl won't teach him to hate me."
Mrs. Errol's voice broke. "I only hope his grandfather will love him."
Mr. Havisham stayed silent. He couldn't imagine the grumpy, old earl loving anybody.
While Mr. Havisham was visiting Mrs. Errol, Cedric was visiting his best friend.
Mr. Hobbs owned the corner grocery store.
As Cedric sat in the store, he thought Mr. Hobbs must be rich to own such a place.
It was filled with so many different kinds of food—from prunes to biscuits.
Mr. Hobbs also owned a horse and wagon for making deliveries.
As for Mr. Hobbs himself, he was annoyed by most people.
But he always enjoyed Cedric's company.
That day he was reading aloud from the newspaper while Cedric perched on a stool.
"Look at this picture from England!"
Mr. Hobbs held up the paper so Cedric could see a ceremony at Queen Victoria's palace.
"All those earls, sitting around doing nothing."
"Have you known many earls, Mr. Hobbs?" Cedric asked.
"I should say not!" Mr. Hobbs replied indignantly.
"They're all tyrants. I won't have any of them sitting around here wearing their fancy velvet robes and coronets."
"What's a coronet?" Cedric asked.
"A little crown," Mr. Hobbs said with disgust.
Cedric was familiar with Mr. Hobbs' poor opinion of the British.
They had been the enemy during the American Revolution.
He also knew that Mr. Hobbs especially disliked the aristocracy.
"Maybe earls wouldn't want to be earls if they knew it was a bad thing," Cedric said.
"Ha! They love being earls! Everybody else does all their work.
Why would they give that up?"
They were in the middle of this conversation when Mrs. Errol's servant, Mary, appeared.
Her face was flushed with excitement.
"Come home, darling," Mary said to Cedric. "Your mother needs you."
Cedric slipped off the stool. "Does she want me to take a walk with her?"
Mary shook her head. She had such an odd look on her face that Cedric immediately began to worry.
"Is something wrong with Mama?" Cedric asked.
"Has the hot sun given her a headache?"
"No, but something unusual has happened. Come along now."
Mary motioned for Cedric to accompany her.
When Cedric reached home, he was puzzled to see a carriage waiting in front of his house.
"Hurry upstairs and put on your best clothes!" Mary said.
As Cedric passed the parlor door, he noticed his mother sitting on the sofa.
She was talking to a stranger, who sat perfectly straight in his chair.
The stranger looked very serious.
Mrs. Errol heard his footsteps. "There's Cedric," she said to Mr. Havisham.
"He's back from visiting his good friend Mr. Hobbs."
"Who's Mr. Hobbs?"
"The owner of the grocery store."
"Of course," Mr. Havisham said quietly.
Once again he wondered what kind of boy Cedric was.
In his world, gentlemen's sons didn't make friends with grocers.
When Cedric came downstairs, he was wearing a cream-colored suit.
Mary had neatly combed his blond curls.
"Oh, Cedric!" Mrs. Errol held out her arms.
Cedric ran to his mother and gave her a hug.
The tall stranger rose from his chair and studied Cedric from head to toe.
"So this is Lord Fauntleroy!"
"I'm sorry, sir, but you're mistaken. I'm Cedric Errol."
Cedric went over and shook the man's hand.
Mr. Havisham couldn't help smiling at this boy who acted like an adult.
"I'm Mr. Havisham, the Earl of Dorincourt's lawyer."
Cedric's eyes widened. "You know a real earl?
Wait until I tell Mr. Hobbs. We were just talking about earls!"
"Come sit next to me." Cedric's mother patted the sofa.
"Mr. Havisham has some news for you."
For the next hour, Mr. Havisham and Mrs. Errol went over the story with Cedric.
He kept repeating, "You mean, [i@I'll@i] be a real earl someday?"
As the two adults continued to talk, Cedric listened quietly.
When Mary brought tea, Cedric passed the cookies to Mr. Havisham before taking one himself.
Mr. Havisham was impressed with his good manners.
"What a charming, friendly child he is," Mr. Havisham thought.
"I'm still not sure I understand all this," Cedric said as Mr. Havisham stood up to leave.
"You will understand in time," Mr. Havisham said.
"I think you'll find it's quite nice to be an earl. You'll be extremely wealthy one day."
After the front door closed, Cedric gave his mother a mournful look.
"I don't want to leave New York. There has to be a way out of this, Mama!"
"I'm sorry, Cedric," Mrs. Errol said.
"Your grandfather has sent for you, and you must go.
I believe it's what your father would have wanted.
The news is a shock to me, too, but at least I'll be coming with you."
Cedric hung his head. "None of my friends are earls. I don't know why I have to be one."
"I'll be sorry to leave Mr. Hobbs," Cedric told his mother at breakfast the next morning.
"I'll miss all my friends, but especially him. And he'll miss me."
"I understand, Cedric," Mrs. Errol said.
"I'll miss my friends and Mary and this little house . . ."
Her voice trailed off, and a tear rolled down her cheek.
Cedric got up and gave her a hug. "We'll manage, Mama."
As soon as the grocery store opened, Cedric went to see Mr. Hobbs.
"Good morning!" the grocer said, setting aside his newspaper.
"Hello," Cedric said mournfully.
He didn't climb onto his usual stool but stood with his hands in his pockets.
He dreaded breaking the news to his friend.
"Mr. Hobbs, do you remember what we were talking about yesterday?" Cedric said.
"Hmm," Mr. Hobbs said. "I think it was England."
"Yes, but when Mary arrived . . . what were we discussing then?" Cedric asked.
"Let's see." Mr. Hobbs rubbed his chin. "Queen Victoria and the aristocracy."
"And earls. You said you wouldn't have any earls sitting around here, wearing their robes and coronets."
"That's right!" Mr. Hobbs said. "And I called them tyrants too!"
"I forgot that part." Cedric turned bright red with embarrassment as he took a seat on a barrel.
"Well, Mr. Hobbs, an earl is sitting here right now."
The grocer almost jumped out of his chair. "What?"
"Yes, [i@I@i] am an earl—or rather I'm going to be one."
Mr. Hobbs hurried to check the thermometer in the front window.
"It's a hot day, and the heat has gone to your head.
How do you feel?" Mr. Hobbs asked with concern. "Do you hurt anywhere?"
He laid his hand on Cedric's forehead. "Poor Cedric," he thought.
"Something is very wrong with him today!"
"Thank you, but I'm all right," Cedric said.
"I'm just sorry to say I'm really going to be an earl. That's why Mary fetched me.
The earl's lawyer traveled all the way from England to tell my mother."
Mr. Hobbs sank into his chair and mopped his face with his handkerchief. "One of us has heatstroke!"
"No, we're both fine. Now let me tell you what the lawyer said."
Mr. Hobbs listened carefully as Cedric told the story of how he became Lord Fauntleroy.
When Cedric finished, the grocer asked, "Who's your grandfather?"
Cedric pulled a paper from his pocket.
"I wrote down his name because I couldn't remember it all.
John Arthur Molyneux Errol, Earl of Dorincourt.
And that's who I'll be someday, the Earl of Dorincourt."
Mr. Hobbs let out a low whistle. "What did you say your name is now?"
"Lord Fauntleroy."
Mr. Hobbs looked amazed. "Well, isn't that something!"
"England is very far away, isn't it?" Cedric said.
"Oh my, yes. It's across the Atlantic Ocean."
"That's the worst part," Cedric said. "I probably won't see you for a long time."
The two friends sat quietly for a few minutes, thinking about that.
Finally Mr. Hobbs spoke. "Are you sure you have to be an earl?"
Cedric nodded sadly. "I'm sure. All I can do is try to be a good one."
Cedric spent a long time talking to Mr. Hobbs.
On his way home, he saw some of his friends.
They were taking turns racing against each other.
"Come on, Cedric!" one boy called.
"Join us! You can race Billy to the lamppost by your house."
Cedric quickly forgot about being an earl and joined Billy at the starting line.
At just this moment, Mr. Havisham's carriage pulled into Cedric's street.
Mr. Havisham signaled for the driver to stop so he could watch the race.
"Ready, set, go!" the first boy called, and the racers took off.
"Come on, Lord Fauntleroy!" Mr. Havisham said quietly.
Cedric ran as fast as he could and touched the lamppost two seconds before Billy.
"Bravo, Lord Fauntleroy!" Mr. Havisham said more loudly this time.
"Three cheers for Cedric!" the boys cried, surrounding their friend.
Cedric noticed Billy standing off to the side by himself. "Hey, Billy, come here!"
The winner put his arm around the loser.
"You know why you lost, Billy? It's simple.
My legs are longer than yours, and I'm three days older than you.
That gave me a huge advantage."
Billy slowly smiled. "Yes, Cedric, I'm sure you're right."
Mr. Havisham's smile turned into a frown.
"Cedric is such a kind boy," he thought.
"It's a pity he has to live with the earl. He has no idea how hard that will be."
There was something else Cedric didn't know yet.
When he moved to England, he'd be living apart from his mother.
Mrs. Errol seemed flustered when Mr. Havisham and Cedric arrived.
"I'm sorry, Mr. Havisham," she said, "but I must speak to my servant.
Mary has just received some terrible news."
Mrs. Errol hurried into the kitchen, leaving Cedric to entertain the lawyer.
Mr. Havisham sat in a chair while Cedric took a seat opposite him.
Mr. Havisham wasn't used to talking to children and had no idea what to say.
Cedric finally broke the silence. "I don't really understand what an earl is.
And when a boy is going to be one, he ought to know."
Mr. Havisham was relieved. This was a topic he could talk about.
"Earls are important men," the lawyer began.
"Over the centuries they've helped to govern England.
They usually come from very old families and—"
Cedric popped up from the sofa with excitement.
"The woman who sells apples is very old! She must be close to a hundred!"
"Well . . . an old [i@person@i] is not the same as an old [i@family@i].
The first Earl of Dorincourt received his title almost four hundred years ago."
"Oh, I see." Cedric sat down.
They fell into silence again. Mr. Havisham studied a crack in the wall.
Cedric sighed. "Sometimes I wish I had lots of money."
Mr. Havisham raised his eyebrows. "What would you do with it?"
"I'd buy the apple seller a tent for her stall and a stove and a warm shawl.
She's so poor that she has to work every day, even when it's raining."
Cedric stopped to think. "And on rainy days, I'd give her a dollar so she could stay home!"
Mr. Havisham smiled at his generosity. "Why would you do all that?"
"Because she's been kind to me," Cedric explained.
"When I fell and cut my knee, she gave me an apple for free."
"That was kind," Mr. Havisham agreed.
He suddenly found himself enjoying this conversation. "What else would you do?"
"I'd like to help my friend Dick.
He's just a few years older than I am, but he has a shoeshine stand with a partner.
Once I had a new ball that bounced into the street.
Dick ran after it and brought it back. We've been friends ever since."
Cedric frowned. "The shoeshine business isn't too good right now."
Mr. Havisham forced himself not to smile at Cedric's knowledge of the shoeshine business. "And why is that?"
"Well, everybody likes Dick, but nobody likes his partner.
Jake's a bad guy. I wish Dick could have his own shoeshine stand."
Mr. Havisham leaned forward. "What about you? Is there anything you want?"
Cedric grinned. "A pony! Sometimes when Mama and I are walking, we see a boy riding. I'd like to ride!"
Just then Mrs. Errol came into the parlor, looking upset.
"Mary's husband is sick, and now he's lost his job."
"I must talk to her!" Cedric slipped from the sofa and left the room.
"That's quite a boy you have," Mr. Havisham said to Mrs. Errol.
"There will be many changes in his life. One day he'll have lots of power—"
"Oh, he's just a little boy!
I hope I can teach him to use his power wisely." Mrs. Errol seemed distressed.
"Cedric will have lots of money too," Mr. Havisham went on.
"The earl wants me to buy whatever he wants.
But Cedric only wants to help others. I don't think that's what the earl had in mind."
Mrs. Errol gave a sympathetic sigh. "That poor, lonely man.
His sons have died, and now he just wants to be kind to my boy."
Mr. Havisham couldn't look her in the eye. The earl was far different from what she imagined.
The earl's motive was to ensure that Cedric would come to England.
"Give my grandson whatever he wants," the earl had told Mr. Havisham.
"I don't care what you spend. Make sure he has money in his pocket and knows it came from me."
Cedric walked slowly back into the parlor.
"Mary doesn't know how they'll pay the rent," he said sadly.
"Their landlord is threatening to evict them. I wish we could help them."
Mr. Havisham made a quick decision.
He reached into his pocket and handed some money to Cedric.
"I'm sure the earl would want Mary to have this."
"Twenty-five dollars!" Cedric's eyes widened in amazement.
"That's a fortune!" Mrs. Errol said.
Running toward the kitchen, Cedric called out, "Mary! Look what I have for you from my grandfather!"
He returned a few minutes later, a big smile on his face.
"I never saw anybody cry with joy like Mary just did," Cedric said.
"Maybe being an earl won't be so bad after all!"
The next few days were exciting ones for Cedric.
First, he took Mr. Havisham to meet the apple seller.
"I have to go to England and be a lord," Cedric explained to the old woman.
"While I'm away, I don't want to worry that you're cold or wet."
Then he told her what he wanted to give her: a tent, a stove, a warm shawl, and money for rainy days.
The apple seller was so astonished that she almost fell over.
Mr. Havisham and Cedric helped her sit on an empty crate.
"What have I done to deserve this?" she kept repeating.
"You gave me an apple when I hurt my knee," Cedric said. "Who could forget that?"
"Many people wouldn't remember," Mr. Havisham said to himself.
The apple seller smiled up at Cedric. "You're such a good boy.
I wish I had something to give you in return. Oh, I know!"
When Cedric and Mr. Havisham walked away, they each carried a shiny red apple.
Their next stop was the shoeshine stand where Dick worked.
When they arrived, Dick was very upset.
"What's wrong?" Cedric asked.
"That Jake! I've just been having more trouble with him."
Dick paced in front of the stand, describing their latest argument.
Cedric was so excited that he could hardly contain himself.
"But, Dick!" he interrupted when he couldn't wait any longer.
"You don't have to be partners with Jake anymore."
Dick halted. "What are you talking about?"
Cedric explained how he'd become a lord, and that his grandfather, the earl, had sent Mr. Havisham to New York.
"My grandfather wants me to have anything I want," Cedric said.
"So I decided I want you to have your own shoeshine stand!"
Dick listened to all this with his mouth open.
"Wait just a minute," he finally said.
"You can't fool me. This is all a joke, right?"
Cedric laughed. "Nobody believes me at first.
Mr. Hobbs thought I had sunstroke.
But I'm telling the truth. Right, Mr. Havisham?"
"Indeed it's all true." Mr. Havisham nodded solemnly.
Like the apple seller, Dick had to sit down to absorb the news.
"Nobody's been this kind to me since my brother, Ben, moved to California. He always took care of me."
"There's more," Cedric said. "I'm giving you money for supplies and new clothes too."
Dick stood up and shook Cedric's hand. "I can't believe my good fortune."
"Well, good-bye, Dick." Cedric's voice trembled slightly, and he blinked back tears.
"I hope business will be good now that you're on your own.
I hate to leave you, but I have to go to England.
Maybe I'll come back for a visit when I'm an earl."
Cedric fished for something in his pocket. "Here's my address. I hope you'll write to me.
But, remember, my name isn't Cedric Errol anymore. It's Lord Fauntleroy."
Dick took the slip of paper from Cedric and blinked hard.
"I wish you weren't going away," he said in a husky voice.
Then Dick turned to Mr. Havisham. "Thank you, sir, for bringing Cedric to see me.
He's a funny little fellow, but I like him very much."
In a daze Dick watched them leave—a small, eager boy chatting away to a tall, serious man.
"I must do something to thank Cedric," Dick said.
Until the day of his departure, Cedric spent as much time as possible with Mr. Hobbs.
Gloom had settled over Cedric's best friend and his store.
When Cedric brought him a gold watch and chain, Mr. Hobbs didn't know what to say.
He laid the watch on a counter and blew his nose several times.
"There's something written inside." Cedric urged Mr. Hobbs to open the case.
"I told the engraver what to write."
Cedric read the inscription aloud.
[i@From Lord Fauntleroy to Mr. Hobbs. When this you see, remember me.@i]
"I don't want you to forget me," Cedric explained.
"I won't forget you." Mr. Hobbs' voice sounded husky, just as Dick's had.
"Don't you forget me when you're among the aristocracy."
"I'll never forget you, no matter who I'm with," Cedric said.
"I've had some of my happiest times with you."
Cedric was sure that his grandfather would invite Mr. Hobbs to visit.
"You won't mind that he's an earl, will you, Mr. Hobbs?" Cedric asked.
"I mean, you wouldn't turn down his invitation just because he's an earl?"
"I'll always come to see you," Mr. Hobbs said.
"Then it's all settled!" Cedric said cheerfully.
"I'll tell my grandfather all about you and ask him to invite you to his castle!"
At last it was time for Cedric and his mother to set sail for England with Mr. Havisham.
After their trunks had been taken to the steamship, a carriage arrived.
Cedric had a strange feeling in his stomach.
His mother had been in her room for some time, but now she came downstairs.
Her eyes were red, and her mouth trembled.
Cedric hugged her, and after they stepped into the carriage, he sat close to her.
"It's very sad to leave all our friends and this little house," he said.
She turned for one last look at their house and nodded. "Yes, we were happy here."
Mr. Havisham stared at his shoes.
He didn't know if Cedric and his mother would be happy in England.
Onboard the ship Mr. Havisham hurried to his cabin.
Cedric and his mother stood on the upper deck, watching the hustle and bustle below.
Carriages dropped off passengers. Trunks and suitcases were dragged about and dropped.
Wherever Cedric looked, there was something new and interesting to see.
Mrs. Errol looked up. "My goodness, those masts are tall."
"Sailors climb all the way to the top," Cedric said.
"I hope I can talk to some of them."
"Oh, Cedric!" His mother laughed.
"By the time we land, I'm sure you'll have talked to everyone on board."
The ship was almost ready to sail when Cedric noticed someone forcing his way through the crowd.
He was carrying something red.
Suddenly Cedric recognized him. "Dick! Over here!"
Breathlessly, Dick ran to Cedric and tipped his cap to Mrs. Errol.
"Business has been great since I got my own stand. So I bought this for you."
Dick thrust a red silk handkerchief into Cedric's hands.
It was decorated with purple horseshoes and horse heads.
"Wear it when your grandfather has a big party."
A bell rang, and Dick darted away before Cedric could thank him.
As the gangplank was removed, Cedric spotted him standing on the wharf and waving his cap. "There's Dick!"
Cedric leaned forward and waved his new handkerchief. "Thank you, Dick! Good-bye!"
Somewhere at sea, Cedric's mother finally told him that they wouldn't be living together.
"What do you mean?" Cedric cried frantically. "Why are we being separated?"
"Don't worry," Mrs. Errol said, smoothing Cedric's hair.
"My house isn't far from the castle.
You can pop in whenever you like and talk to me.
Your father loved Dorincourt Castle, so I'm sure you'll love it too."
"I'd like it a lot better if you were there," Cedric grumbled.
Whenever Cedric brought up the subject, his mother repeated the same comforting words.
He grudgingly accepted the situation, although he thought it was strange.
Meanwhile he made friends with everyone, just as his mother had predicted.
He begged the sailors to tell him stories about pirates.
He took walks around the decks with the ladies.
He joined the men when they talked business in the lounge.
And he led the other children in fun and games.
Everyone knew of Cedric's rise to the English aristocracy, and everyone liked him.
One day Mr. Havisham joined Mrs. Errol for a walk around the upper deck.
"Where's Lord Fauntleroy?" he asked.
"Some sailors are teaching him to tie knots." She laughed.
"If he weren't an earl's heir, I think he'd like to be a sailor!"
Mr. Havisham grunted. "Has he adjusted to the idea that he'll be living at the castle with the earl?"
"He's still puzzled."
"Perhaps you should tell him why this plan was made," Mr. Havisham said.
Mrs. Errol shook her head in disagreement.
"It's better that Cedric doesn't know that the earl hates me.
He'll have a better relationship with his grandfather."
"Are you sure?" Mr. Havisham asked.
Mrs. Errol stared at the endless ocean.
"Cedric is so loving, and I'm so dear to him.
He'd be shocked and hurt to find out that someone dislikes me so much.
No. It's better that he doesn't know until he's older."
Later that day Cedric sat with Mr. Havisham in the lounge.
"I don't like it!" Cedric said when Mr. Havisham mentioned his new living arrangement.
"But I'll try to accept it. Mr. Hobbs and Mary told me that there are many troubles in life that you just have to bear."
"Are you going to like the earl?" Mr. Havisham asked.
"Of course." Cedric nodded. "We're family."
"And do you think he'll be fond of you?"
"I think so because I'm his son's little boy."
Cedric twirled one of his golden ringlets around his finger.
"He must be fond of me, or he wouldn't have sent for me, right?"
Mr. Havisham stayed silent.
It was dark when the carriage arrived at Mrs. Errol's cottage near Dorincourt Castle.
Cedric waited while Mr. Havisham helped his mother from the carriage.
Then he followed them to the door, which was opened by a servant.
Cedric looked around the main room.
Two comfortable chairs sat on either side of the fireplace.
Paintings covered the walls.
Pretty, decorative objects sat on the mantel and the tables.
"I'm glad you're going to live here," Cedric said to his mother.
"This house is so big and comfortable!"
"Yes, but it'll be different from our New York house."
Mrs. Errol remembered sadly how Cedric's smile lit up that house.
A white cat was sleeping in a chair.
Cedric immediately began to make friends with it.
"The housekeeper at the castle thought you might like a cat, ma'am," the servant said.
"So you won't be lonely."
Mrs. Errol's weary face brightened. "Oh, yes, a cat makes a house more home-like."
"Dinner will be ready soon," the servant said, leaving the room.
Mr. Havisham and Mrs. Errol stood talking quietly in a corner.
Cedric was so busy playing with the cat that he didn't listen.
"Cedric doesn't have to go tonight?" she said hopefully.
"He'll stay with me one more night?"
"That's correct," Mr. Havisham said.
"After we've dined, I'll go to the castle and inform the earl of our arrival.
Cedric will meet him tomorrow."
Mrs. Errol looked fondly at her son sitting with the cat.
"The earl doesn't know how much he's taking from me."
She straightened up with a look of resolve.
"Please tell him that I don't want the money."
Mr. Havisham was puzzled. "You mean the monthly allowance he proposed to give you?"
"Yes, I'm grateful for this house, because it means I can be near Cedric.
But I have enough money of my own to live on.
I'd rather not take the earl's money, because he dislikes me so." She shuddered.
"I'd feel like he's bribing me to agree to this arrangement."

Mrs. Errol's face darkened. "He'll understand after a while.

Mr. Havisham thought this over.

Later in the evening, Mr. Havisham arrived at the castle.
A footman led him to the library, where the earl sat in an easy chair by the fire.
His foot was propped up on a special stool to ease his gout pain.
"Havisham, you're back." The earl looked around. "Where's the boy?"
"He's spending one last night with his mother," the lawyer said as he sat down.
"Go on," the earl prodded. "What sort of lad is he?"
Mr. Havisham didn't give many details; he wanted the earl to make up his own mind about Cedric.
"His lordship is a fine boy, but you'll find him different from most English children."
"I'm sure." The earl snorted.
"He's probably an obnoxious American brat with bad manners."
Mr. Havisham rarely disagreed with his employer.
It was an especially bad idea when the earl was suffering from gout.
So there was a long silence.
Finally Mr. Havisham said, "I have a message for you from Mrs. Errol."
"I don't want any of her messages." The earl growled.
"The less I hear from her, the better."
"This is an important one," Mr. Havisham said. "She doesn't want any of your money."
The earl leaned forward. "What did you say?"
"She says she doesn't need the money, and as relations between you are strained—"
"Strained? I'll say they're strained," the earl shouted.
"I can't stand her! She's just a greedy American!"
The lawyer shook his head. "You can hardly call her greedy when she's asked for nothing."
The earl waved his hand to dismiss that argument.
"She's just trying to trick me into visiting her.
She thinks I'll admire her principles, but I won't!
She'll soon be telling everyone she lives like a pauper because I don't give her any money.
Well, she'll have that money whether she spends it or not!"
The earl was breathless with anger and excitement.
"I suppose she's turned the boy against me."
"Actually she has another message for you.
Please don't tell him that you hate her.
She doesn't want to give him a reason to dislike you."
"What?" The earl sank back in his chair in surprise. "You mean she hasn't told him?"
Mr. Havisham shook his head.
"Lord Fauntleroy's feelings about you will depend entirely on your actions."
Late the following afternoon, Mr. Havisham came for Cedric in the earl's carriage.
Cedric was sad to leave his mother.
But when he went outside, he was immediately fascinated by the carriage.
"Did you ever see such beautiful horses?" Cedric asked Mr. Havisham.
"The earl's stable is full of magnificent horses," the lawyer replied.
Cedric squinted at a design on the door.
"That little crown with the big [i@D@i] above it—is that a coronet?"
"Yes, and the [i@D@i] stands for Dorincourt."
"Oh, that's so people realize the earl is inside." Cedric looked at Mr. Havisham.
"Or somebody the earl knows—like you."
"Or you." Mr. Havisham gave a curt nod.
A man in uniform held open the door.
"Mr. Havisham, who's that?" Cedric whispered.
"A servant called a footman. There are more footmen at the castle.
Now hurry up and get in. You don't want to be late for your first meeting with your grandfather."
It took only a few minutes to reach the gate of the great park surrounding the castle.
Cedric peered out the window at a pair of stone lions guarding the entrance.
A woman and two boys came out of an ivy-covered cottage.
While the mother opened the gate, the boys waved to Cedric.
Then their mother curtseyed and smiled at him.
"I don't know those people," Cedric said, "but they act like they know me."

Cedric took off his cap and waved. "Good afternoon!" he called out.
The woman's smile grew even broader. "Welcome, your lordship!"
Cedric turned to Mr. Havisham. "That woman looks as if she likes children.

Mr. Havisham didn't tell him that a young lord doesn't play with a gatekeeper's children.
There was plenty of time for Cedric to learn the rules of his new life.
The carriage rolled down a broad avenue with tall trees on either side.
It passed masses of ferns and flowers.
Cedric pointed excitedly out the window.
"There's a whole herd of deer! Who do they belong to?"
Mr. Havisham smiled at Cedric's delight. "The earl—and one day, you."
"What would Mr. Hobbs think of that?" Cedric said.

"Several miles away."
Cedric settled back against the seat cushions.
"That's a long way for somebody to live from his front gate."
As the castle came into view, the setting sun turned its windows to gold.
"Ohh." Cedric sighed. "It's just like a king's palace in a fairy tale."
Inside the castle a line of servants was waiting to greet Cedric.
At the front of the line stood a kind-looking woman.

Cedric looked around with great interest as a footman escorted him to the library.
The footman opened the door and announced, "Lord Fauntleroy."
Cedric entered a splendid room filled with books and heavy furniture.
The room was so dark that Cedric thought no one was there.
Then he saw someone sitting in the easy chair by the fire.
The man didn't bother to look up.

They all despised him. In fact, 35 years had passed since he'd last seen his only sister.
Cedric took a seat near the earl. "Any boy would love his grandfather, especially one who's been so kind."
The earl was startled. "What do you mean?" he demanded.
"You say that I've been kind to you?" The earl repeated his question to Cedric in the castle library.
Dougal, the earl's dog, sat next to Cedric's chair.
"Oh, yes! I'm forever grateful to you for helping the apple seller and Dick and Mary."

Cedric explained what he'd done for his friends.
While Cedric talked, the earl quietly observed the dog.
"Dougal usually doesn't make friends quickly," the earl thought.
"But he liked this young fellow right away."
At that moment the big dog put his head on the boy's knee.
Cedric petted him while continuing to talk.

"I'm going to keep it forever."
Cedric admired the handkerchief again before returning it to his pocket.
"And this Dick is one of your acquaintances, is he?" the earl asked.
"He's an old friend. Well, not quite as old as Mr. Hobbs," Cedric said.
"Oh! I haven't told you about Mr. Hobbs the grocer—my best friend."
The earl couldn't imagine what Cedric would say next.

Cedric continued talking about the grocer. "I bought Mr. Hobbs a gold watch.

"Dinner is served, my lord," he said.

"Are you sure you could support me?"

"All right, you may try," his grandfather replied.

Usually this was the footman's job.
If the earl felt any pain in his foot, he relieved it by shouting at the footman.
But this time he didn't shout—even when his foot hurt.

The earl didn't hesitate to rest his weight on Cedric.

When they entered the dining room, Cedric's heart sank.

"Perhaps the heat from the fireplace helps your foot."
Cedric wiped his forehead with Dick's handkerchief.

The earl noted Cedric's courage and his respectful attitude.

Cedric wiped his face again.
"It wasn't too hard, but a person does get warm in the summer."

"Please tell the cook that the soup is delicious."

Half an hour later, Mr. Havisham entered the library.
Before he could speak, the earl hushed him.
Cedric and Dougal were fast asleep in front of the fire.

For a moment she stood looking at the sleeping child.

Cedric stood nearby, impatiently waiting for his pony to arrive.

Everyone in the countryside grew used to seeing Lord Fauntleroy on his brown pony.
One afternoon Cedric noticed a boy limping home from the village school.

When they reached his cottage, his mother came to the gate.

Instead he made Cedric tell him the story again.
A few days later, Cedric delivered the crutches while the earl stayed in the carriage.
When Cedric returned to the carriage, he was shaking his head in disbelief.
"Grandpapa, it was just like when you helped Mary.
The boy's mother was crying with happiness," he said.
"I told her you sent the crutches.
You didn't tell me to say that, but I thought maybe you forgot. That was right, wasn't it?"
The earl laughed and didn't contradict his grandson.
On Sunday a crowd waited outside the church before the service.
Reverend Mordaunt stood at the door.
"There are more people than usual today," he said to the village shopkeeper.
"We've all heard a rumor that the earl is bringing Lord Fauntleroy to church," she said.
"Everybody wants to see the boy who'll one day own everything around here."
Reverend Mordaunt gave the shopkeeper a polite smile.
"The earl hardly ever comes to church," the minister thought.
"He probably just wants to show off his grandson."
The crowd parted to let a young woman walk up the path to the church.
The shopkeeper studied the stranger carefully.
"That must be Lord Fauntleroy's mother."
"Yes, I believe it is," Reverend Mordaunt said.
It took Mrs. Errol a few moments to realize that people were staring at her.
As she walked to the church, she was thinking of Cedric.
Yesterday he'd ridden his pony all the way to her cottage.
She smiled at the memory.
But her thoughts were interrupted by a woman in a red cloak.
"Good morning, my lady!" the woman said, curtseying.
Other women followed her example and curtsied.
One man after another removed his hat as Mrs. Errol passed.
Mrs. Errol felt puzzled. Then she blushed when she realized what was going on.
"They're doing this because I'm Lord Fauntleroy's mother!" she thought.
"Good morning!" she said shyly and bowed in return.
Having always lived in America, she wasn't used to this type of attention.
"It's embarrassing, but everyone means well," she thought.
"I'm touched by how friendly the villagers are."
Mrs. Errol had barely entered the church when the earl's carriage drove up the lane.
"Here they come!" The news passed excitedly from one group to another.
The carriage came to a stop, and a footman opened the door.
A boy in a black velvet suit and hat jumped out.
Every man, woman, and child stared at him.
They didn't bother trying to hide their curiosity.
"He looks just like the captain!" said a woman who remembered Cedric's father.
As a footman helped the earl from the carriage, Cedric looked at his grandfather affectionately.
"The earl of Dorincourt doesn't frighten that lad!" one man said with a chuckle.
"Just lean on me," Cedric said to his grandfather. "Everyone is so happy to see you!"
"Take off your cap!" the earl ordered his grandson as he leaned on the boy's shoulder.
"They're bowing to you."
"To me?" Cedric whipped off his hat and tried to bow to everyone at once.
"They've heard how you helped that poor farmer," the earl said.
The earl hadn't cared about the farmer.
But it had amused him to let Cedric help the man.
He also enjoyed that Cedric was popular with the tenants.
"Good morning, Lord Fauntleroy!" cried the woman in the red cloak. "Long may you live!"
"Thank you, ma'am!"
Cedric led his grandfather into the church.
When they sat down, Cedric was pleased to see his mother seated across the aisle.
Cedric smiled at her, but the earl didn't even glance in her direction.
"I hope Cedric will always be a good person," Mrs. Errol thought, watching her son and the earl.
"Especially when he's the earl and has so much power over these people."
After church Cedric walked home with his mother.
As they sat down for lunch, Cedric noticed the fresh flowers on the table.
"Flowers and fruit arrive every day from the castle," Cedric thought.
"So Grandpapa must be fond of Mama. But I still don't understand why they've never met."
Before he could ask anything, Mrs. Errol brought up the thoughts she'd had at church.
"Cedric, I hope you'll always be brave, honest, and kind." She unfolded her napkin.
"Then you won't hurt anyone, and you'll help many people.
The world will be a better place because you were born."
Cedric ran around the table to hug her. "I'll try, Mama," he said.
"The world is a better place because Grandpapa's alive.
That's for sure! When I grow up, I'll try to be just like him."
After Cedric had returned to the castle, he told the earl about the conversation with his mother.
"I said that you've made the world a better place, and that I want to be just like you," Cedric said.
The earl shifted uneasily in his chair. "What did your mother say about that?"
"She said that was right. And that we must always look for the good in people and imitate it."
The earl was too surprised to reply.
He had never expected such a kind response from Cedric's mother.
A few days later, Cedric was leaving the castle to visit his mother.
He expected to ride in the earl's carriage, pulled by two horses.
Instead a small carriage with one horse and a driver waited for him.
"That's a present for your mother," said the earl, who had followed Cedric outside.
"She shouldn't walk to church or anywhere else she wants to go."
"Oh, Grandpapa!" Cedric could hardly contain his excitement.
"You're the kindest man in the world!
Wait until Mama sees her own horse and carriage!"
Then Cedric noticed that the earl wasn't dressed to go visiting.
"Where's your hat, Grandpapa? Where are your gloves?
You're coming with me, right? I'm sure Mama will want to thank you in person."
The earl shook his head. "Tell your mother this is a present from [i@you@i]. Now hurry back here."
Cedric climbed into the carriage and called out the window.
"Are you sure you won't come along?"
"Yes, and remember that this is a present from you, not me."
Cedric was always eager to see his mother.
But that day the short ride to her house seemed longer than usual.
"I wish the driver could make the horse go faster," Cedric thought.
When they finally arrived at the cottage, Cedric's mother was cutting flowers in the front garden.
"Mama! Look what I brought you!" Cedric called from the carriage.
Cedric's mother approached the carriage with a bouquet in her arms.
"It's your own carriage!" Cedric said proudly.
"Whenever you want to go somewhere, this man will drive you."
Mrs. Errol looked up at the man holding the horse's reins. He tipped his hat to her.
"Grandpapa said I must tell you that it's a present from me!" Cedric said.
"Even though I know it's really from him. Isn't he the kindest man in the world?"
"It's a beautiful carriage." Mrs. Errol reached out to pat the horse.
She didn't want to accept this gift from the earl.
But she also didn't want to spoil her son's happiness.
"Let's go for a ride." Cedric hopped from the carriage and held open the door.
"I must put these flowers in the house first."
Cedric insisted, however, that they go right that minute.
So Mrs. Errol let herself be taken for a drive.
The whole time Cedric happily talked about his grandfather.
By the time they returned home, his mother had a better attitude toward the earl.
"I'm glad you see the goodness in your grandfather."
Mrs. Errol put her arm around her son. "He has so few friends."
"You're wrong, Mama! Everyone likes Grandpapa."
That night Cedric wrote a letter to his friend Mr. Hobbs, the grocer.
Cedric described his rooms and the castle and the park.
He talked about learning to ride. But he mostly wrote about his grandfather.
[i@You said all earls were tyrants, but my grandfather isn't one.@i]
[i@In fact, I think you'd like him.@i]
[i@So far I haven't seen his velvet robe and coronet.@i]
Then he wrote about his mother.
[i@Most of the time I'm happy living with my grandfather.@i]
[i@Except when I miss my mother. I wish she could live at the castle with me.@i]
After Cedric finished his letter, he showed it to the earl.
"Would you check the spelling for me?"
The earl slowly read both sides of the paper.
When he finished, he asked, "Do you miss your mother very much?"
"I miss her all the time." Cedric laid a hand on the earl's arm.
"But you don't miss her, do you?"
"I don't know her at all," the earl said.
"I've always wondered about that, but Mama told me not to ask you any questions."
Cedric paused, hoping the earl would say more.
When the old man stayed silent, Cedric said, "I won't ask you again. Good-night."
For a while Mr. Hobbs pretended that Cedric hadn't really gone away.
He was sure that one day his young friend would reappear.
But, of course, that didn't happen.
Cedric's letter made the grocer miss his friend even more.
Mr. Hobbs read and reread the letter.
He folded it up and sighed. "I'll never forget you, Cedric."
That night Mr. Hobbs slowly walked down the street to the house where Cedric had lived.
There was still a For Rent sign in the front window.
Mr. Hobbs stared at the house before returning to the store.
"I wish I had someone to talk to." Mr. Hobbs took Cedric's letter from his pocket.
"It would be nice to share this with someone. But I don't know who that would be."
The earl continued to shower Cedric with gifts.
Another boy might become spoiled, but Cedric was still under his mother's influence.
So he remained the same thoughtful, unselfish boy he'd always been.
Cedric and the earl were becoming good friends.
On sunny days the earl watched Cedric's riding lessons.
On rainy days they stayed inside and played the baseball game together.
One rainy day the earl's doctor came to visit.
Cedric put away the baseball game.
Then he played quietly with Dougal while the two men talked in the library.
"You haven't mentioned your gout lately," the doctor said to the earl.
"Is your foot bothering you?"
"Now that you mention it . . ." The earl paused.
"I haven't noticed the pain as much."
"Perhaps that's because you have other things to think about."
The doctor gestured toward Cedric.
"Well, perhaps," the earl said in a gruff voice.
The earl didn't like to admit to others that they were right.
But he admitted to himself that time passed more quickly when Cedric was around.
The next day was sunny, so Cedric and the earl went to the stables together.
"I wish you'd go riding with me," Cedric said.
"It would be such fun if you'd ride too."
"Fun, you say? Hmm." For a moment the earl looked thoughtful.
Then he summoned the head groom.
"Wilkins, saddle my horse! I'm taking Lord Fauntleroy riding this morning."
"But you haven't ridden in years," Wilkins said. "Are you sure, my lord?"
"Don't just stand there!" The earl started to turn purple with rage.
"Lord Fauntleroy and I are waiting!"
"I just—I mean—yes, my lord!"
Wilkins was flustered by the earl's unexpected order.
"It'll only take a few minutes, my lord."
After that the earl rode with his grandson almost every day.
As they traveled along the country roads, Cedric chatted away.
Much of the time, he talked about his mother.
The earl soon learned that Mrs. Errol led a busy life.
"Everyone knows her and loves her," Cedric said proudly.
"It's a good thing my mother has her own carriage!
She's always visiting anybody who needs help.
She brings food to the poor and sits with the sick and the lonely.
There are even some children who come to her house to learn to sew!"
The earl didn't like to hear Cedric talk about his mother.
But he was curious about one thing.
"Why does your mother do so much for people she hardly knows?" he asked.
"Oh, that's easy." Cedric smiled up at his grandfather.
"We didn't have much money in New York. But now she feels rich!
So she wants to help anyone she can."
By this point the two riders had reached an overlook.
From here they had a wide view of everything below and the castle in the distance.
The earl made a sweeping gesture that took in the whole scene.
"Do you know that all this land belongs to me?" he asked Cedric.
"That's a lot of land to belong to one person!"
"And one day it will all belong to you."
Cedric was awestruck. In a quiet voice, he asked, "When?"
"When I am dead."
"Then I don't want it!"
Cedric was horrified at the thought of his grandfather's death.
"I wish you'd live forever."
"That's a kind thought," the earl said.
"Nevertheless, someday it will all be yours, and you'll be the Earl of Dorincourt."
Cedric sat very still for a few moments.
He gazed at the broad moors, the green farms, and the pretty village.
Above the trees he could see the towers of the castle. Then he sighed.
"What are you thinking about?" the earl asked.
"I was looking at all the houses and thinking about something my mother said yesterday.
She said it's not easy to be an earl.
And that I must learn about the people who live on my land.
That way I'll be able to help them."
Cedric sighed again at the thought of all that responsibility.
"So, Grandpapa, how did you learn about everybody?
The earl flushed.
He only knew which tenants paid their rent and which ones had to be evicted.
He hadn't bothered to learn anything more about the people who lived on his land.
"Reverend Mordaunt tells me what's going on," he finally said.
"When you're an earl, Cedric, make sure you're a better one than I am."
On the ride home, the earl thought about his past.
He wished he'd led a better life.
He would hate for Cedric to know the truth—he was known as "the wicked Earl of Dorincourt."
From a distance the village looked beautiful.
But Mrs. Errol knew that everything was not as lovely as it seemed.
On some streets the cottages were in bad shape, and the residents were often sick.
One day Mrs. Errol happened to meet Reverend Mordaunt on one of the worst streets.
"Look at these cottages," she said. "Some of them are nearly falling down.
Tenants have told me their roofs are leaking.
And I've seen the damp walls and broken windows when I've visited the sick."
"It's a shame." Reverend Mordaunt shook his head.
Mrs. Errol watched some children playing in the dirt.
"I worry about the children who live here.
Meanwhile my son lives in a castle, surrounded by a beautiful park.
He's treated like a prince and can have whatever he'd like."
"You're right. It's not fair," Reverend Mordaunt agreed.
"Many times I've asked the earl to do something about these cottages, but he doesn't seem to care."
"I wonder . . ." Mrs. Errol tapped her foot as she looked around.
"The earl will do whatever Cedric wants.
If I tell Cedric that these cottages need to be replaced, and he tells the earl—"
Reverend Mordaunt smiled. "Then the cottages will be replaced!"
A few days later, Cedric entered the library.
He didn't greet the earl but went straight to a big chair and sat down.
Lost in thought, he frowned and sighed.
"You look troubled," the earl said. "Is something bothering you?"
Cedric nodded solemnly.
"When I visited my mother yesterday, she told me about a horrible place in the village.
She cried when she described the cottages where the poor families live.
Their houses are collapsing!"
Cedric got up and leaned against the earl's chair.
"You said that Reverend Mordaunt tells you about the people who live on your land.
But he must have forgotten to mention this place.
If he had, I know you would have helped."
The earl looked uncomfortable as Cedric continued.
"I promised Mama I'd make sure you knew."
Cedric looked up hopefully at his grandfather.
At that moment the earl realized that Cedric was the only person who'd ever trusted him.
Suddenly the earl was ashamed of the miserable cottages.
He was also ashamed to admit that he'd known about them for years.
"What do you think I should do?" the earl asked.
"Mama says those cottages must be knocked down and rebuilt.
So that's what you should do." Cedric's face brightened.
"Let's tell the tenants tomorrow!"
"It may not be tomorrow." The earl laughed.
"But the tenants will have new cottages."
When work on the cottages began, Cedric and his grandfather rode to the village almost every day.
Cedric quickly made friends with the workmen.
One day two men were laying bricks.
"I like learning about new things," Cedric said to the earl.
"Would you mind holding my pony while I talk to these men?"
The earl watched with pride as the men greeted Cedric.
A few minutes later, Cedric returned to tell the earl everything he'd learned about laying bricks.
"He's a good boy," one bricklayer said to the other as they watched Cedric ride away.
"He'll make a fine earl someday."
The second man nodded. "Lord Fauntleroy is already making a difference.
He has a good effect on the old earl."
That night Cedric sat on the library rug with Dougal.
"Do you remember the night I arrived?" he asked the earl.
"I said two people would be lonely living here if they weren't good friends.
I think we're good friends now."
"We are pretty good friends," his grandfather admitted. "Come here."
Cedric scrambled to his side, and the dog followed.
"Is there anything you want?" the earl asked.
"Well . . . ," Cedric began slowly.
"I know we're friends, but I really wish I lived with my mother."
The earl winced. "You see her almost every day. Isn't that enough?"
"But I used to see her first thing in the morning and last thing at night.
She was always there, so we had lots of time to talk."
Cedric locked eyes with his grandfather. Neither said anything for a moment.
Then the earl scowled. "Do you ever forget about your mother?"
"Never! And she never forgets about me either." Cedric patted his grandfather's arm.
"Now that I know you, I wouldn't forget about you if we lived apart.
I'd probably think about you even more."
His grandfather nodded. "I believe you would!"
Although the earl had grown fond of Cedric, he couldn't enjoy this warm moment with his grandson.
He was too busy feeling jealous of Mrs. Errol.
But the earl soon had worse problems.
There hadn't been a celebration at Dorincourt Castle for years.
But now the earl wanted to throw a grand dinner party to show off his grandson.
He had no idea that bad news would arrive that night.
The earl invited all the lords and ladies he knew.
He even invited his sister, Constantia, to visit.
They'd quarreled 35 years ago, and he hadn't seen her since.
Constantia arrived a few days before the party.
The first thing she wanted was to meet Cedric.
"I've heard the boy has worked miracles on you, John," she teased her brother.
"Some of the tenants have even stopped calling you 'the wicked Earl of Dorincourt.'"
The earl scowled. "I don't know about that."
His face brightened when Cedric entered the library. "Come here, Cedric!"
The boy ran to his grandfather, who held out a hand to a lady with white curls and friendly eyes.
"I'd like you to meet your great-aunt, Lady Constantia."
Cedric shook her hand. "I'm pleased to meet you, Great-Aunt Constantia."
Constantia smiled warmly at him.
"I was always fond of your papa, and you remind me so much of him."
"It makes me happy when people say that, because everyone liked him," Cedric said.
"Everyone likes my mother too. While you're here, I hope you can meet her."
"I hope so too." Constantia raised her eyebrows at the earl, who looked away.
"The workmen are putting a new roof on a cottage," Cedric said to his grandfather.
"Do you want to ride over to watch?"
"Another time," the earl said. "Wilkins will take you riding today."
After Cedric left the library, the earl and his sister sat down for tea.
"You couldn't have found a better heir."
Constantia poured the tea. "You must be pleased."
"He's a fine fellow, and we're great friends."
The earl started to smile. "I've actually become quite fond of him."
"What does his mother think of you?"
The earl's smile faded into another scowl. "I haven't asked her."
"I must be frank with you, John, and say that I don't approve of what you've done.
It's wrong to separate the child from his mother." Constantia put down her teacup.
"I intend to call on her tomorrow.
So if you're going to quarrel with me, you'd better do it now."
The earl had forgotten that his sister never hesitated to say what she thought.
"From what I've heard," Constantia said, "she has been a wonderful influence on her son.
I've also heard that your tenants adore her."
"They adore [i@him@i]." The earl corrected his sister.
"You can go see her, if you like. Just don't try to make me visit her!"
The next day Constantia returned from visiting Mrs. Errol.
"She's a perfectly lovely person," Constantia told her brother.
"You should thank her for making Cedric the fine boy that he is."
The earl harrumphed at Constantia.
But she noticed he didn't say anything bad about Mrs. Errol.
The dinner party was that night. Cedric put on his best black velvet suit.
Before he went downstairs to the ballroom, he stuffed Dick's handkerchief into a pocket.
"I wish Dick could see me wearing this to a party," he said to himself.
At the party all the guests wanted to talk to Cedric.
They smiled when he showed them Dick's red-and-purple gift.
They were charmed by his kindness toward the earl.
Constantia watched as Cedric followed his grandfather around the ballroom.
"John's own sons never paid him this much attention," she thought.
"No wonder John enjoys his company."
Soon a footman approached the earl. "Should I announce that dinner is served, my lord?"
The earl looked at his watch and frowned.
"Mr. Havisham isn't here yet. Has there been any word from him?"
"No, my lord."
"This is most unusual. Mr. Havisham is always on time."
The earl checked his watch again.
"We'll wait a few more minutes. Let me know the moment his carriage arrives."
The footman turned and spotted the tall lawyer entering the room.
"Mr. Havisham has arrived, my lord."
"Yes, I can see that," the earl said impatiently.
"Good evening, Mr. . . .," Cedric started to call out.
"Havisham, where have you been? Why are you late?" the earl demanded. "What's wrong?"
Mr. Havisham, who was never agitated, was pale and obviously upset.
Before the lawyer could reply, a second footman arrived at the earl's side.
"Cook says dinner will be ruined if it's not served immediately."
"Then announce that dinner is served!" the earl snarled.
"Havisham! Tell me what's wrong at once!"
Mr. Havisham glanced around uneasily at the guests.
"Not here. You'll want to hear the news in private."
At dinner Mr. Havisham was lost in thought.
He ate hardly anything, and whenever anyone spoke to him, he seemed startled.
"What?" he said more than once.
Cedric, who was sitting next to the earl, smiled at the lawyer.
But Mr. Havisham just gave him an anxious glance.
"Something's wrong with my friend Mr. Havisham," Cedric thought.
"He always smiles at me. I hate to see him so worried."
Meanwhile Mr. Havisham felt more distressed every time he looked at Cedric and the earl.
"What terrible news I have to give them!" he thought. "It will ruin their lives forever."
After dinner Cedric joined the ladies in the drawing room.
The men stayed in the dining room to talk.
The earl raised his eyebrows at Mr. Havisham, inviting him to speak.
But the lawyer shook his head.
"Not yet," he whispered.
By the time the men joined the ladies, Cedric was sleepy.
Leaning back on a soft sofa cushion, he closed his eyes.
He vaguely heard guests saying goodnight to the earl.
The earl had been growing more and more uneasy.
And when he was uneasy, he was always in a bad mood.
After the last guest had left, he turned on Mr. Havisham.
"Well, what's this news that you've brought me? And why have you made me wait all evening?"
"It's bad news, my lord," Mr. Havisham said carefully as the two men sat down.
"The worst news. And I'm sorry to be the bearer of it."
Mr. Havisham glanced over at Cedric, who was asleep and unaware that his life was about to change.
"Why do you keep looking at the boy like that?" the earl demanded.
"I saw you watching him at dinner. What does your news have to do with him?"
"It has everything to do with Lord Fauntleroy," Mr. Havisham said.
"I was late tonight because a woman came to see me. She told me an extraordinary story."
Mr. Havisham paused before making his dramatic announcement.
"It seems that Cedric is not the real Lord Fauntleroy!"
"That's nonsense!" The earl snorted.
"Of course he's the real Lord Fauntleroy."
Mr. Havisham looked over at Cedric again.
"The real Lord Fauntleroy is the son of your older son, Bevis.
At the moment he's staying with his American mother at an inn in the village."
The earl gripped the arms of his chair. Veins stood out on his hands and his forehead.
"Who told you this lie?" he said angrily. "Bevis didn't have any children when he died."
"That's what we thought," Mr. Havisham said.
"But this woman said Bevis married her six years ago in London.
She showed me her marriage certificate, which appears to be real.
Then she said she had a five-year-old son."
The earl was too shocked to say anything, so Mr. Havisham went on.
"Soon after the boy's birth, Bevis and this woman decided to separate.
He paid her a sum of money to disappear."
"That sounds like something Bevis would do," the earl admitted.
"He was always irresponsible, a total disgrace to the family.
What is this woman like?"
"For a while she didn't realize what her son was entitled to.
But she recently consulted a lawyer and learned that the boy is your heir."
The lawyer shuddered. "She's uneducated, totally greedy, and only cares about money."
The earl took out his handkerchief and mopped his face. He gestured toward Cedric.
"And to think that I objected to this dear boy's mother.
I took her child away and then refused to have anything to do with her."
The earl shook his head. "I suppose this is my punishment," he said bitterly.
Suddenly he rose from his chair and began to pace the room.
He raged about Bevis and his horrible American wife.
But he never spoke loudly enough to wake Cedric.
Broken and haggard, the earl approached the sofa and stood over Cedric.
"If anyone had told me I could be fond of a child, I wouldn't have believed them.
I always disliked children, especially my own.
But I am fond of this one, and he is fond of me."
The earl brushed the hair from Cedric's forehead, and the boy stirred.
"Cedric would've been a better earl than I've been.
No one would've called him the 'wicked Earl of Dorincourt.'
He would've brought honor to the family."
For a moment the earl bent down and studied Cedric's happy, sleeping face.
Then he rang for a footman.
When the footman appeared, the earl pointed to the sofa.
"Carry—" The earl's voice cracked with emotion. "Carry Lord Fauntleroy to his room."
Back in New York, Mr. Hobbs was still missing Cedric.
It was the end of the day, and the grocer was sitting alone in his store.
"No one can take Cedric's place," Mr. Hobbs thought.
"But it would be good to talk to someone besides myself.
Cedric was always mentioning another friend of his—Dick.
Maybe Dick's looking for a new friend too."
The next day Mr. Hobbs went for a shoeshine at Dick's stand.
He wasn't quite sure how to start the conversation.
"This is a nice stand," Mr. Hobbs finally said.
"A friend of mine set me up in business."
Dick applied some polish to Mr. Hobbs' shoes.
"He was the best little guy you ever met.

"Would that be Lord Fauntleroy?"
Dick was so surprised that he dropped his cloth.
"Yes! Do you know Cedric too?"
"I've known him since he was born. I'm Mr. Hobbs, the grocer."
Dick shook Mr. Hobbs' hand enthusiastically.
"Cedric told me all about you!"
Mr. Hobbs grinned. "And I feel like I already know you."
"I miss Cedric." Dick picked up his cloth and went back to polishing Mr. Hobbs' shoes.
"Whenever I was feeling down, he always cheered me up."
"Me too." Mr. Hobbs nodded in agreement.
Cedric's friends soon realized they had a lot to discuss.
Mr. Hobbs invited Dick to visit him the next evening.
After that the two quickly became friends.
They enjoyed reading Cedric's letters aloud and writing to him.
Dick often needed help writing letters.
One night he looked over Mr. Hobbs' shoulder while the grocer edited his letter.
"I didn't have much schooling because I was always working.
I got a job as soon as I was old enough to sell newspapers and run errands."
Mr. Hobbs handed Dick's letter back to him.
"Why did you start working so young?"
"After my parents died, my brother, Ben, took care of me.
He had a job in a store, but we both needed to make money.
Everything was fine until he married Minna."
Dick rolled his eyes. "I guess he liked her because she was pretty with long, dark hair.
But she had such a terrible temper!"
After Minna had a baby, she sometimes made Dick take care of him.
"When baby Tom cried, Minna would throw things at [i@me@i]!" Dick said.
"Like it was my fault that her baby was screaming!"
"She sounds dreadful," Mr. Hobbs said.
"Once she threw a plate at me and hit the baby instead!

Dick shook his head as if he still couldn't believe the story.
"The doctor said Tom would always have that scar."

[i@I am not a lord, and I won't be an earl when my grandfather dies.@i]

Cedric's mother was busy writing a letter when her servant interrupted.
